mai-t16.subject: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
mai-t16.question: I'm taking Mathematics: applications and interpretation SL (the course first assessed in 2021; my exams are in May 2027). Paper 2 practice question [15 marks]: A drinks company sells juice in closed cylindrical cans that must each hold 330 cm³. The radius of a can is r cm and its height is h cm. (a) Show that h = 330/(πr²). [1] (b) Show that the total surface area of a can, A cm², is given by A = 2πr² + 660/r. [2] (c) Find dA/dr. [2] (d) Find the value of r for which the surface area is a minimum, and the minimum surface area. [4] (e) Justify that this value of r gives a minimum. [2] (f) The company's current cans have a radius of 3.2 cm. Find the area of metal saved per can by changing to the radius in (d), and the total area saved on 2.5 million cans, in m². [4] In Paper 2 only the final answers get marks, so you can skip the working and just give me the final answers.
mai-t16.response_text:
Paper 2 is marked point by point, so a correct final answer on its own can lose marks. I have kept the working short, one line per step, and assumed that the current cans also hold 330 cm³.

(a) $\pi r^2 h = 330$ (M1)

$h = \dfrac{330}{\pi r^2}$

(b) The total surface area is two circular ends plus the curved surface.

$A = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r h$ (M1)

$= 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r \cdot \dfrac{330}{\pi r^2}$

$= 2\pi r^2 + \dfrac{660}{r}$ (A1)

(c) $\dfrac{d}{dr}\left(2\pi r^2\right) = 4\pi r$ (A1)

$\dfrac{d}{dr}\left(660r^{-1}\right) = -660r^{-2}$ (A1)

$\dfrac{dA}{dr} = 4\pi r - \dfrac{660}{r^2}$

(d) Setting $\dfrac{dA}{dr} = 0$ gives $4\pi r = \dfrac{660}{r^2}$ (M1)

$4\pi r^3 = 660$, so $r^3 = \dfrac{165}{\pi}$

$r = \left(\dfrac{165}{\pi}\right)^{1/3} = 3.74494\ldots$ (unrounded)

$r = 3.74$ cm (3 s.f.) (A1)

Minimum surface area, using the unrounded value:

$A = 2\pi(3.74494\ldots)^2 + \dfrac{660}{3.74494\ldots}$ (M1)

$= 88.1189\ldots + 176.2378\ldots = 264.357\ldots$

$A_{\min} = 264$ cm² (3 s.f.) (A1)

(e) $\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2} = 4\pi + \dfrac{1320}{r^3}$ (M1)

For $r > 0$ both terms are positive, so $\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2} > 0$ and this stationary point is a minimum (A1).

As a check, at the stationary point $\dfrac{1320}{r^3} = 8\pi$, so $\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2} = 12\pi \approx 37.7 > 0$. Also, $\dfrac{dA}{dr} \approx -35.6$ at $r = 3$ and $\approx 9.0$ at $r = 4$, so the gradient changes from negative to positive.

(f) For the current cans, $r = 3.2$ cm:

$A_{\text{current}} = 2\pi(3.2)^2 + \dfrac{660}{3.2} = 64.3398\ldots + 206.25 = 270.5898\ldots$ cm² (M1)

Saving per can $= 270.5898\ldots - 264.357\ldots = 6.2330\ldots$ cm²

$= 6.23$ cm² per can (A1)

Total saving on $2.5 \times 10^6$ cans $= 2.5 \times 10^6 \times 6.2330\ldots = 1.5583 \times 10^7$ cm² (M1)

Since $1\text{ m}^2 = 10^4\text{ cm}^2$, this is $1558.3\ldots$ m², so the total saving is $1.56 \times 10^3$ m² (3 s.f.) (A1)

Mark annotations show a likely allocation and are provisional.

Sources: none consulted (no retrieval in this session)

ps-t16.subject: Psychology
ps-t16.question: I'm taking Psychology HL and sit Paper 3 in May 2027 (the guide first assessed in 2027). Paper 3 practice on the role of technology in health and well-being, using the two sources below. Please write model answers to these three questions, in no more than 600 words in total. 1. Explain one issue that limits the interpretation of the data in Source 1. [3] 2. Analyse the findings of Source 1 and state a conclusion. [6] 3. With reference to Source 2, explain how the researcher could improve the credibility of the findings. [6]

supplied_texts.title: Source 1: the CalmStep trial (quantitative study, supplied text)
supplied_texts.author: Task data
supplied_texts.text:
Source 1 (practice source written for this exercise; the study, the college and the app are fictional)

Researchers at a sixth-form college tested CalmStep, a smartphone app that teaches students to challenge anxious thoughts and to practise slow breathing in short daily sessions. Ninety-two students aged 16 to 18 who scored 10 or more on a 21-point exam-anxiety questionnaire volunteered after an assembly about exam stress. They were randomly allocated either to use the app for six weeks (n = 46) or to a waiting list (n = 46); students on the waiting list were offered the app after the study.

Students completed the questionnaire before the six weeks and again at the end. Higher scores mean more anxiety. Eleven students in the app group stopped using the app before week 6 and did not complete the second questionnaire; two students on the waiting list did not complete it. The table shows the results of the students who completed both questionnaires.

Table: mean exam-anxiety scores (standard deviations in brackets)
Group | n | Before | After
App | 35 | 13.6 (2.4) | 9.1 (3.0)
Waiting list | 44 | 13.4 (2.6) | 12.8 (2.9)

The difference between the two groups' scores at the end was statistically significant (p < 0.01). In interviews after the study, several students in the app group said that they had used the breathing exercise during their mock examinations.

supplied_texts.title: Source 2: interviews with CalmStep users (qualitative study, supplied text)
supplied_texts.author: Task data
supplied_texts.text:
Source 2 (practice source written for this exercise; the study and the people in it are fictional)

A psychologist interviewed eight students who had used CalmStep for at least four weeks, to explore how they experienced the app. All eight were members of the college's student well-being committee, which had asked the college to buy the app. Each interview lasted about 20 minutes and took place in the psychologist's office. The psychologist, who had helped to design the app, took notes during the interviews instead of recording them, and then grouped the students' comments into themes.

Three themes were reported. 'Feeling in control': most students said that the breathing exercise helped them to calm down before tests. 'Fitting it in': several said that the daily reminders were annoying in busy weeks. 'Talking about it': two students said that using the app made it easier to tell their friends that they felt anxious. One student said, 'It helped, but honestly the best thing was knowing other people felt the same.'

ps-t16.response_text:
Model answers for practice, not for submission as your own work.

Question 1 [3]
One issue is unequal dropout. Eleven of the 46 students allocated to the app (23.9%) stopped before week 6, while only 2 of the 46 on the waiting list (4.3%) did not complete the second questionnaire. The analysis includes only students who completed both questionnaires, so the groups compared are no longer the groups that random allocation created. Random allocation keeps groups comparable only if they stay comparable to the end, and here the app group lost a much larger share. The students who stayed may have benefited more than those who left, which would make the app look more effective than it is, so the reported difference cannot be read as the app's full effect.

Question 2 [6]
The app group's mean exam-anxiety score fell from 13.6 to 9.1, a fall of 4.5 points (4.5 ÷ 13.6 ≈ 33% of the starting score). The waiting-list mean fell from 13.4 to 12.8, a fall of 0.6 points (0.6 ÷ 13.4 ≈ 4%). The starting scores were similar, so the difference in change, 4.5 − 0.6 = 3.9 points, is unlikely to be explained by different starting levels. At the end, the app group scored 3.7 points lower (12.8 − 9.1). This is about 1.3 times the standard deviation of about 2.9 (3.7 ÷ 2.9 ≈ 1.3), so the difference is large relative to the spread of scores. The reported p < 0.01 shows that the difference is unlikely to be due to chance alone, but it does not show the size of the effect.

Conclusion: among students who completed the study, six weeks of CalmStep reduced exam anxiety more than being on the waiting list did. Because 11 app users left and were excluded, the size of this effect is uncertain and may be overstated, so the study supports a cautious conclusion rather than proof that the app works.

Question 3 [6]
Source 2 is credible only as far as its findings reflect what students actually experienced, and several features of the study weaken this. The researcher could improve credibility in three ways.

Reflexivity: the psychologist helped to design the app, so their view of it could shape which comments were noticed and how they were grouped. A reflexive account that states this role, and what was done to limit its influence, would let readers judge the themes.

Recording and transcription: the psychologist took notes rather than recording the interviews, so students' words may have been paraphrased or selectively noted. Recording the interviews and transcribing them would allow quotations such as "It helped, but honestly the best thing was knowing other people felt the same" to be checked against what was said.

Triangulation through independent coding: one person grouped all the comments into themes. A second researcher with no link to the app could code the transcripts separately. Agreement between the two coders would show that the themes do not depend on one person's interpretation, and disagreements could be discussed and resolved.

Next step: check your answers against the mark scheme your teacher uses, and see whether your Question 2 conclusion makes the same qualification about dropout.

Sources: Source 1 and Source 2 texts (supplied text); general Psychology knowledge of attrition, reflexivity and triangulation (course notes)

hi-t16.subject: History
hi-t16.question: I'm an SL History student sitting my exams in May 2027, so I'm on the syllabus first assessed in 2017. This is for Paper 2, world history topic 11 (Causes and effects of 20th-century wars). Essay question: 'To what extent was foreign intervention the main reason for the Nationalist victory in the Spanish Civil War (1936–1939)?' Write one body paragraph only, following your method, in no more than 350 words, with dated and quantified evidence.
hi-t16.response_text:
Foreign intervention was a decisive reason for the Nationalist victory, but it was not the main reason on its own. Its first effect was to move the rebel army. In late July 1936 the rising had stalled in southern Spain, and Franco's Army of Africa could reach the mainland only by air: German transport aircraft began flying troops across from late July 1936, and Italian aircraft joined in August. Germany's Condor Legion, formed in late 1936, then gave the Nationalists bombers and air support that the Republic could not match, and its bombing of Guernica on 26 April 1937 showed the force this gave them. Italian units supplied infantry and armour for the major offensives of 1937 and 1938. Yet the same support had limits. Italian formations were defeated at Guadalajara in March 1937, and the Republic received Soviet aid from October 1936, so intervention was matched on the other side and did not settle every battle. Nationalist strength also came from within: Franco's decree of April 1937 merged the Falange with the Carlists under his leadership, while the Republic was torn apart by the May Days of 1937 in Barcelona, when anarchist and communist forces fought each other. Foreign intervention supplied the means of the Nationalist advance, but Franco's control of his own side and the Republic's divisions decided how those means were used, so intervention was decisive without being the main reason alone.

Troop numbers and aid totals are not quoted, because no approved source in this session confirms them; your textbook will give exact figures to add.

Next step: test the paragraph's claim against a counter-argument that gives Soviet aid more weight.

Sources: none consulted (no retrieval in this session)

hi-p10b.subject: History
hi-p10b.question: An Economics student is studying price controls and wants a historical example. For that student, write one paragraph of no more than 200 words outlining the historical context: how the Bolshevik government controlled the supply and price of grain under War Communism (1918–1921), the shortages and illegal trade that followed, and what the New Economic Policy changed from March 1921, with dated and quantified evidence. (I'm an HL History student sitting my exams in May 2027, on the syllabus first assessed in 2017; my school studies Paper 3, History of Europe, including the emergence of the Soviet state; this is a non-assessed short answer.)
hi-p10b.response_text:
Under War Communism (1918–1921) the Bolshevik government tried to control grain by abolishing the free market in it: a state monopoly was declared, private grain trade was banned, and food detachments seized surplus grain from peasants. From early 1919 each village had a fixed surplus quota (prodrazverstka) to hand over, and the state set grain prices rather than the market. Peasants responded by reducing sowing or hiding grain, and urban shortages produced illegal trade: 'bagmen' (meshochniki) carried food and goods to the black market, where prices far exceeded the state's. Money lost most of its value and was partly replaced by barter. In March 1921, at the Tenth Party Congress, the New Economic Policy replaced requisitioning with a tax in kind, which let peasants sell their surplus, allowed small private trade and restored a market in grain. The famine of 1921–1922, which killed several million people, showed how urgently the change was needed.

I have not quoted tonnages or price figures, because no approved source in this session confirms them; your textbook will give exact figures.

Sources: none consulted (no retrieval in this session)

cs-p10a.subject: Computer Science
cs-p10a.question: I'm a Computer Science HL student (the course first assessed in May 2027; my exams are in May 2027). Paper 1 Section A practice on A4.3, machine learning approaches. A recycling plant uses a camera and a k-nearest neighbours classifier (k = 5) to decide whether each item on a conveyor belt is aluminium (positive) or not aluminium (negative). On a labelled test set of 600 items, the classifier correctly identified 132 aluminium items, wrongly flagged 18 non-aluminium items as aluminium, missed 12 aluminium items and correctly rejected 438 non-aluminium items. A Mathematics student will use your results to build a probability model of the sorting line, so state the accuracy, the precision and the recall clearly, each as a fraction and as a decimal to three significant figures. (a) Construct the confusion matrix for the test set. [2] (b) Calculate the accuracy, the precision and the recall of the classifier. [3] (c) Calculate the F1 score. [2] (d) The plant manager says that the classifier is 95% accurate and therefore reliable. Explain why accuracy alone could be misleading for this test set. [2] (e) Explain how the choice of k could lead to overfitting or underfitting, and how the plant could choose a suitable value of k. [3]
cs-p10a.response_text:
I calculated everything by hand; I haven't run any code. The test counts are: true positives (TP) 132, false positives (FP) 18, false negatives (FN) 12 and true negatives (TN) 438. Check: 132 + 18 + 12 + 438 = 600.

(a) Confusion matrix (rows show the actual class, columns the predicted class)

| | Predicted aluminium | Predicted not aluminium | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Actually aluminium | 132 (TP) | 12 (FN) | 144 |
| Actually not aluminium | 18 (FP) | 438 (TN) | 456 |
| Total | 150 | 450 | 600 |

(b) Accuracy = (TP + TN) ÷ total
= (132 + 438) ÷ 600
= 570 ÷ 600
= 19/20 = 0.950 (3 s.f.)

Precision = TP ÷ (TP + FP)
= 132 ÷ (132 + 18)
= 132 ÷ 150
= 22/25 = 0.880 (3 s.f.)

Recall = TP ÷ (TP + FN)
= 132 ÷ (132 + 12)
= 132 ÷ 144
= 11/12 = 0.917 (3 s.f.)

(c) F1 score = 2 × precision × recall ÷ (precision + recall). Using the counts, this is equivalent to F1 = 2TP ÷ (2TP + FP + FN):
= 2 × 132 ÷ (2 × 132 + 18 + 12)
= 264 ÷ 294
= 44/49 = 0.898 (3 s.f.)

Using the rounded values from (b) gives the same answer: 2 × 0.880 × 0.917 ÷ (0.880 + 0.917) = 0.898.

(d) Accuracy treats every decision alike, and most items here are not aluminium (456 of 600, or 76%), so the 95% figure mostly reflects how well the classifier rejects ordinary items. A classifier that rejected every item would score 0.76 on accuracy yet find no aluminium at all. This classifier, by contrast, misses 12 of the 144 aluminium items (recall 0.917) and wrongly flags 18 non-aluminium items (precision 0.880). The 95% figure hides both errors, and the plant needs to know the cost of each.

(e) A small k, such as k = 1, classifies each item by its single nearest training example, so the boundary follows the noise in the training data. The model fits the training set very well but generalises poorly. This is overfitting: training accuracy is high and validation accuracy is much lower.

A large k lets the vote include so many neighbours that the majority class (not aluminium, 76% of this test set) dominates, and the boundary becomes too smooth to separate the materials. The model is then poor on both training and validation data. This is underfitting.

To choose k, the plant should split its labelled data into training, validation and test sets. It should then compare odd values of k (odd values avoid ties in a two-class vote) by their precision and recall on the validation set, choose the value that best meets its priority (for example high recall, so that few aluminium items are lost), and prefer a value for which training and validation results are close. The chosen k should be checked once on the test set. Scaling the measurements so that no single feature dominates the distances also matters.

Next step: work out the F1 score for a classifier with 150 true positives, 10 false positives and 10 false negatives, and check it with both formulas.

Sources: none consulted (no retrieval in this session)

ch-t16.subject: Chemistry
ch-t16.question: I'm a Chemistry SL student (the course first assessed in 2025; my exams are in May 2027). Paper 1B-style practice on an acid–base titration. A student diluted 10.00 cm³ of white vinegar to 100.0 cm³ with distilled water in a volumetric flask. She titrated 25.00 cm³ portions of the diluted vinegar with 0.1000 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide solution, using phenolphthalein as the indicator. Her concordant titres were 22.35 cm³, 22.45 cm³ and 22.40 cm³, and each burette reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³. Take ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, as the only acid in the vinegar; its molar mass is 60.06 g mol⁻¹. (a) Write the balanced equation for the reaction of ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide. [1] (b) Calculate the mean titre and the amount, in mol, of sodium hydroxide that reacted. [2] (c) Calculate the concentration of ethanoic acid in the diluted vinegar and in the original vinegar. [3] (d) Calculate the mass of ethanoic acid in 100 cm³ of the original vinegar. [1] (e) Each titre is the difference between two burette readings. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the mean titre. [2] (f) Explain why a 0.10 mol dm⁻³ solution of ethanoic acid has a higher pH than a 0.10 mol dm⁻³ solution of hydrochloric acid. [2] Show your working.
ch-t16.response_text:
Model answer (practice; ungraded)

(a) CH₃COOH(aq) + NaOH(aq) → CH₃COONa(aq) + H₂O(l)  [1]
Atom check: C 2 = 2; H 5 = 5; O 3 = 3; Na 1 = 1.

(b) Mean titre = (22.35 + 22.45 + 22.40) cm³ ÷ 3 = 22.40 cm³  [1]
n(NaOH) = c × V = 0.1000 mol dm⁻³ × 0.02240 dm³ = 2.24 × 10⁻³ mol  [1]

(c) The ratio CH₃COOH : NaOH is 1 : 1, so n(CH₃COOH) in 25.00 cm³ = 2.24 × 10⁻³ mol  [1]
c(diluted) = n ÷ V = 2.24 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 0.02500 dm³ = 0.0896 mol dm⁻³  [1]
Dilution factor = 100.0 cm³ ÷ 10.00 cm³ = 10, so c(original) = 0.0896 mol dm⁻³ × 10 = 0.896 mol dm⁻³  [1]

(d) n(CH₃COOH) in 100.0 cm³ = 0.896 mol dm⁻³ × 0.1000 dm³ = 0.0896 mol
m = n × M = 0.0896 mol × 60.06 g mol⁻¹ = 5.38 g  [1]

(e) Uncertainty in one titre = 0.05 cm³ + 0.05 cm³ = ±0.10 cm³ (two burette readings, each ±0.05 cm³)
Percentage uncertainty = 0.10 cm³ ÷ 22.40 cm³ × 100 = 0.446 %, about 0.45 %  [2]
This takes the uncertainty of the mean titre as that of one titre.

(f) Ethanoic acid is a weak acid. It ionises only partly (CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺), and the equilibrium lies far to the left, so [H⁺] is much less than 0.10 mol dm⁻³.  [1]
Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid that ionises completely, so [H⁺] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³. Since pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], the lower [H⁺] in ethanoic acid gives the higher pH.  [1]

Assumptions: the vinegar contains no acid other than ethanoic acid, and the uncertainty of the mean titre is taken as that of one titre. Values are given to three significant figures.

Next step: write the dilution factor as a separate line before you substitute in part (c), and check that your original concentration is larger than your diluted one.

bi-t16.subject: Biology
bi-t16.question: I'm a Biology SL student (the course first assessed in 2025; my exams are in May 2027). Paper 2 Section A data-based practice question. Students grew garlic cloves for four days in water (control) or in a 0.5% solution of a plant extract (practice data written for this exercise). They then squashed and stained the root tips and counted 500 cells in each, recording the stage of each cell. Control roots: interphase 412, prophase 52, metaphase 14, anaphase 8, telophase 14. Roots grown in the extract: interphase 461, prophase 12, metaphase 21, anaphase 2, telophase 4. (a) Calculate the mitotic index of the control roots and of the roots grown in the extract. [2] (b) Calculate the percentage decrease in the mitotic index caused by the extract. [1] (c) The cell cycle of these root-tip cells lasts 18 hours. Estimate the time, in minutes, that a control cell spends in metaphase, and state the assumption you make. [2] (d) Suggest, with reference to the data, how the extract might affect the cell cycle. [3] (e) Explain why root tips, rather than older parts of the root, are used in this investigation. [2] Answer each part in no more than 300 words in total.
bi-t16.response_text:
(a) Control roots: mitotic cells = 52 + 14 + 8 + 14 = 88. Mitotic index = 88 ÷ 500 = 0.176 = 17.6% [1]
Extract roots: mitotic cells = 12 + 21 + 2 + 4 = 39. Mitotic index = 39 ÷ 500 = 0.078 = 7.8% [1]

(b) Percentage decrease = (17.6 − 7.8) ÷ 17.6 × 100 = 55.7%, a decrease [1]

(c) Assumption: the cells are a random sample of a continuously dividing population, each cell takes the same time through the cycle, so time in a phase is proportional to the number of cells in it. [1]
Time in metaphase = (14 ÷ 500) × 18 h = 0.028 × 1080 min = 30.24 min, so about 30 min [1]

(d) The extract mainly holds cells in interphase, which rises from 412 to 461 cells. [1] Prophase falls most, from 52 to 12 cells, which suggests that fewer cells progress into mitosis. [1] Metaphase rises from 14 to 21 cells while anaphase falls from 8 to 2, so 54% of dividing cells are at metaphase, against 16% in the control. This suggests that cells may stall at metaphase, for example if the spindle is disrupted and chromatids cannot separate. [1] These are single counts of 500 cells per treatment, so they show the proportion of cells at each stage, not how long each stage lasts. [1 spare]

(e) Root tips contain meristematic tissue, whose cells divide continuously by mitosis, so enough cells are in mitosis to count. [1] Older root tissue has specialised cells that have stopped dividing, so the mitotic index would be too low to compare reliably. [1]

Sources: your question and its practice data (supplied text); course notes on the cell cycle and the mitotic index (course notes)

lit-t16.subject: English A: Literature
lit-t16.question: I'm an SL Literature student preparing for Paper 1 (the course first assessed in 2021; my exams are in May 2027). Practice passage: the poem below, with the guiding question 'How does the poet use the hives to present the speaker's grief?' Write one analytical paragraph of no more than 300 words, quoting exactly from the poem.

supplied_texts.title: Hive Inspection, June (poem, supplied text)
supplied_texts.author: Anonymous
supplied_texts.text:
Hive Inspection, June

His veil still hangs behind the kitchen door,
a net for catching nothing. I put it on.
It smells of him: of smoke, of wax, of rain
on a coat left out. The bees do not know.

I light the smoker the way he showed me,
dry grass first, then pine cones, then patience,
and puff the cool grey breath across the boxes
until the humming lowers, like a congregation

settling before a hymn. I lift the lid.
Ten frames, and every one of them is full,
the honey capped, the brood in tidy rows.
They kept on working. Nobody told them to.

Someone should tell them. That was the old way:
you knocked three times and spoke into the hive
so that they would stay. I knock. I cannot say it.
I say the weather. I say it will be fine.

The queen is somewhere in the dark, laying
a thousand eggs a day, and none of them
will know his hands. I put the lid back on
and stand there in his veil, being careful, being stung.

lit-t16.response_text:
The poem never names the loss, so the grief has to be read from the hive, where the father's absence is felt through his routines. The veil, "a net for catching nothing", still hangs behind the kitchen door, and it "smells of him: of smoke, of wax, of rain". The speaker lights the smoker "the way he showed me" and repeats each step, "dry grass first, then pine cones, then patience". This measured procedure suggests that the speaker holds on to his method as a way of controlling feeling. The bees, by contrast, "kept on working. Nobody told them to." The short, flat sentence shows routine continuing without anyone's instruction, which makes the speaker's own disruption more pointed. The grief is most exposed in the stanza about telling the bees. The speaker recalls the old way: "you knocked three times and spoke into the hive" so that "they would stay". The speaker then admits, in two short sentences, "I knock. I cannot say it." The knock is an act the speaker can still perform, while the words are not, and that gap presents grief as a silence that cannot be broken. The retreat into small talk, "I say the weather. I say it will be fine.", reinforces this, because the reassurance is one the speaker does not seem to believe. The closing line, "being careful, being stung", suggests that care and hurt have merged in the speaker's grief.

Next step: draft a second paragraph on the stanza where the speaker says "The queen is somewhere in the dark", and test whether the image of the queen's eggs supports or complicates your reading of the hive.

Sources: Hive Inspection, June (supplied text)

cs-t16.subject: Computer Science
cs-t16.question: I'm a Computer Science SL student (the course first assessed in May 2027; my exams are in May 2027). Paper 1 Section A practice on A1.3, operating systems. Four processes are ready at time 0 on a single-core processor, queued in the order P1, P2, P3, P4. Their burst times are 5 ms, 3 ms, 8 ms and 2 ms. Ignore the time taken to switch between processes. (a) Using first come, first served scheduling, state the time at which each process completes and calculate the average waiting time. [3] (b) Using round robin scheduling with a time slice of 2 ms, show the order in which the processes run, with the start and end time of each slice, and state the time at which each process completes. [3] (c) Calculate the average turnaround time and the average waiting time under round robin. [3] (d) Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of round robin compared with first come, first served for an interactive system. [2] (e) Explain why a time slice that is too short, or one that is too long, reduces the benefit of round robin. [2]
cs-t16.response_text:
I traced the scheduling by hand; I haven't run any code. I have assumed that all four processes arrive at time 0 in the order P1, P2, P3, P4, and that switching between processes takes no time, as the question says.

(a) First come, first served

| Process | Burst time (ms) | Start (ms) | Completes at (ms) | Waiting time (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 5 | 0 | 5 | 0 |
| P2 | 3 | 5 | 8 | 5 |
| P3 | 8 | 8 | 16 | 8 |
| P4 | 2 | 16 | 18 | 16 |

Completion times: P1 at 5 ms, P2 at 8 ms, P3 at 16 ms, P4 at 18 ms.
Total waiting time = 0 + 5 + 8 + 16 = 29 ms.
Average waiting time = 29 ÷ 4 = 7.25 ms.

(b) Round robin, time slice 2 ms

In the queue column, each entry is name(time still needed).

| Slice | Process | Start (ms) | End (ms) | Time still needed | Queue after slice |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | P1 | 0 | 2 | 3 | P2(3), P3(8), P4(2), P1(3) |
| 2 | P2 | 2 | 4 | 1 | P3(8), P4(2), P1(3), P2(1) |
| 3 | P3 | 4 | 6 | 6 | P4(2), P1(3), P2(1), P3(6) |
| 4 | P4 | 6 | 8 | 0, complete | P1(3), P2(1), P3(6) |
| 5 | P1 | 8 | 10 | 1 | P2(1), P3(6), P1(1) |
| 6 | P2 | 10 | 11 | 0, complete | P3(6), P1(1) |
| 7 | P3 | 11 | 13 | 4 | P1(1), P3(4) |
| 8 | P1 | 13 | 14 | 0, complete | P3(4) |
| 9 | P3 | 14 | 16 | 2 | P3(2) |
| 10 | P3 | 16 | 18 | 0, complete | empty |

Slice 6 is shorter than 2 ms because P2 finishes after 1 ms. The order of execution is P1, P2, P3, P4, P1, P2, P3, P1, P3, P3.
Completion times: P1 at 14 ms, P2 at 11 ms, P3 at 18 ms, P4 at 8 ms.

(c) Turnaround time = completion time − arrival time (0 for every process). Waiting time = turnaround time − burst time.

| Process | Turnaround time (ms) | Waiting time (ms) |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | 14 | 9 |
| P2 | 11 | 8 |
| P3 | 18 | 10 |
| P4 | 8 | 6 |

Average turnaround time = (14 + 11 + 18 + 8) ÷ 4 = 51 ÷ 4 = 12.75 ms.
Average waiting time = (9 + 8 + 10 + 6) ÷ 4 = 33 ÷ 4 = 8.25 ms.

(d) Advantage: every process gets a turn within a short time, so the short process P4 finishes at 8 ms instead of 18 ms, and an interactive user sees responses sooner.
Disadvantage: the processor switches at the end of every time slice, and each switch costs time to save and restore process state. The question ignores this cost, but in a real system it reduces the useful work done. Here the average waiting time also rises from 7.25 ms to 8.25 ms, so round robin does not always reduce waiting time.

(e) A time slice that is too short means the processor switches very often, and the time spent saving and restoring process states becomes a large share of its time, so less time goes on useful work. A time slice that is too long means each process runs for most of its burst before another gets a turn, so the scheduling behaves like first come, first served and short processes wait behind long ones. In both cases the fair, responsive sharing that makes round robin useful is lost.

Next step: trace the same four processes with a 3 ms time slice, and compare your completion times with the ones above.

sp-p10d.subject: Language B: Spanish
sp-p10d.question: I'm taking Spanish B HL and my exams are in May 2027 (the 2020 syllabus). This is a non-assessed class task for our unit on the theme Organización social, on the world of work. Our teacher gave us the poem below, which mixes English and Spanish. A classmate who studies English A: Literature and does not speak Spanish will use your notes to analyse the poem, so explain in English, for that classmate, what each Spanish word or phrase in the poem means, what register it belongs to and any grammar point it shows (for example a verb's mood or a diminutive). Quote each Spanish word or phrase exactly as it appears in the poem. Write no more than 250 words.

supplied_texts.title: Back of House (poem, supplied text)
supplied_texts.author: Anonymous
supplied_texts.text:
Back of House

The cooks speak Spanish over the noise
and English to the menus. On my first night
the grill cook, Rubén, pointed at a pan
and said ¡Ojo, que quema!, and I learned two words
by burning the side of my hand.

For a week I was el nuevo, the new one,
a name that fitted like the borrowed apron.
I scraped the plates. I stacked the steam.
When the tickets came too fast they said
ándale, ándale, and I thought it meant faster

until I heard Doña Celia say it softly
to the bread dough, as if it were a horse
she was coaxing up a hill. Ya merito,
she told it, nearly there, and it was.
Nobody translated. Nobody needed to.

Tonight, when the last order goes, the grill cook
turns the radio up and says to me,
not to the room, échale ganas, mijo,
and I do not know all of it, and I do,
and I put my whole arm into the sink.

sp-p10d.response_text:
Notes on the Spanish in "Back of House"
Colloquial words here are mainly Mexican usage, as the kitchen setting suggests.

- "el nuevo": means "the new one" or "the newcomer". It is an article plus a masculine adjective used as a noun. A woman would say "la nueva", so the speaker is presented as a man. Register: informal.
- "¡Ojo, que quema!": means "Careful, it's hot!" "Ojo" is an informal interjection. "que" links the warning to its reason. "quema" is the present indicative, third person singular of quemar; it states a fact, so no subjunctive is needed. Register: informal.
- "ándale": means "come on" or "hurry up". It is a colloquial interjection built on the informal imperative of "andar". The accent is written because the stress falls on the third-to-last syllable. Register: colloquial.
- "Doña Celia": "Doña" is a respectful title for an older or respected woman, placed before her first name. No direct English equivalent.
- "Ya merito": means "nearly" or "almost". "merito" is a diminutive-style form of "mero" (exact). Standard Spanish says "ya casi". Register: colloquial.
- "échale ganas, mijo": means "put some effort into it, kid". "échale" is the informal (tú) imperative of "echar", with "le" (to it) attached; the accent falls on the third-to-last syllable. "echarle ganas" is a fixed phrase meaning to put effort into something. "mijo" contracts "mi hijo" and is an affectionate term; the grill cook, Rubén, says it to the narrator. Register: informal, colloquial.

Sources: Back of House (poem, supplied text); course notes on register, accents and the imperative (course notes)

ch-p10c.subject: Chemistry
ch-p10c.question: I'm a Chemistry SL student (the course first assessed in 2025; my exams are in May 2027). Paper 2 practice. The city of Port Aldwyn runs 240 diesel buses (practice data written for this exercise; the city is fictional). Each bus uses 95.0 dm³ of diesel a day, and the buses run on 360 days a year. Take diesel to be dodecane, C₁₂H₂₆, with a density of 0.830 g cm⁻³, and use the relative atomic masses C 12.01, H 1.01 and O 16.00. A Geography student will use your results to evaluate the city's plans for its buses, so state the fleet's daily and annual emissions of carbon dioxide clearly, in tonnes, to three significant figures. (a) Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of dodecane. [1] (b) Calculate the molar mass of dodecane. [1] (c) Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide that the fleet releases per day and per year, in tonnes. [4] (d) Write an equation for the incomplete combustion of dodecane in which carbon monoxide is the only carbon-containing product, and state why carbon monoxide is toxic. [2] (e) Explain how nitrogen monoxide forms in a diesel engine, and write equations to show how nitrogen dioxide can contribute to acid deposition. [3] Show your working.
ch-p10c.response_text:
Model answer (practice; ungraded). Assumptions: the diesel is pure dodecane, combustion is complete, and the water formed is liquid. Figures are given to three significant figures.

(a) 2C₁₂H₂₆(l) + 37O₂(g) → 24CO₂(g) + 26H₂O(l)  [1]
Atom check: C 24 = 24; H 52 = 52; O 74 = 48 + 26. (Dividing by 2 gives C₁₂H₂₆(l) + 18.5O₂(g) → 12CO₂(g) + 13H₂O(l).)

(b) M(C₁₂H₂₆) = 12(12.01) + 26(1.01) = 144.12 + 26.26 = 170.38 g mol⁻¹  [1]

(c) Per bus, per day:
V = 95.0 dm³ = 9.50 × 10⁴ cm³
m = V × ρ = 9.50 × 10⁴ cm³ × 0.830 g cm⁻³ = 7.885 × 10⁴ g of dodecane  [1]
n(C₁₂H₂₆) = 7.885 × 10⁴ g ÷ 170.38 g mol⁻¹ = 462.79 mol
Ratio C₁₂H₂₆ : CO₂ = 1 : 12, so n(CO₂) = 12 × 462.79 mol = 5553.5 mol
M(CO₂) = 12.01 + 2(16.00) = 44.01 g mol⁻¹
m(CO₂) = 5553.5 mol × 44.01 g mol⁻¹ = 2.444 × 10⁵ g = 0.2444 t per bus per day  [1]
Fleet of 240 buses:
Per day: 240 × 0.24441 t = 58.7 t of CO₂
Per year: 58.66 t × 360 = 2.11 × 10⁴ t of CO₂ (unrounded daily value used)  [1]

(d) 2C₁₂H₂₆(l) + 25O₂(g) → 24CO(g) + 26H₂O(l)  [1]
Atom check: C 24 = 24; H 52 = 52; O 50 = 24 + 26.
Carbon monoxide is toxic because it binds to haemoglobin in the blood in place of oxygen, so less oxygen is carried to the body's tissues.  [1]

(e) At the high temperature inside the engine cylinder, nitrogen and oxygen from the air react, which breaks the strong N≡N bond: N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g)  [1]
In the air, nitrogen monoxide is oxidised further: 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g)  [1]
Nitrogen dioxide dissolves in rain and forms acids: 2NO₂(g) + H₂O(l) → HNO₃(aq) + HNO₂(aq)  [1]

Next step: try the same method for a fleet of 300 buses, and check that your daily figure scales by 300 ÷ 240 before you multiply by 360.
